CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue active negotiations with the US toward a comprehensive deal, while maintaining willingness to make selective purchase commitments (agricultural, energy, semiconductors) but resisting structural concessions on industrial policy and state subsidies. Avoid retaliatory escalation that could trigger the threatened tariff increase from 10% to 25% on $200 billion of goods. Use the negotiation window before the March 1 deadline (now likely extended) to lock in a framework that preserves China's core development model.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not existential at this point. The US has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods (roughly half of US-China trade), and China has retaliated covering nearly all $130 billion of US imports into China (Fox Business). The tariff war is already affecting China's export economy, and the threatened escalation to 25% on $200 billion (from the current 10%) plus potential tariffs on the remaining ~$267 billion would cover virtually all bilateral trade. However, as Brookings notes, more than half the value of China's exports to the US consists of components from other countries (South Korea, Japan), meaning US tariffs also hurt US firms and third-country suppliers — giving China some leverage. The CNBC report from Feb 21, 2019 shows negotiations are actively progressing with six MOUs being drafted on structural issues (forced tech transfer, IP, services, currency, agriculture, non-tariff barriers), and a 10-item purchase list under discussion. This represents the most significant progress in the trade war. China's best move is to continue negotiating in good faith, offer meaningful purchase commitments to reduce the trade surplus, while holding firm on core structural issues like industrial subsidies and Made in China 2025. Retaliating further would be counterproductive given the US threat to tariff all remaining trade. The negotiation track offers the best path to de-escalation while preserving China's strategic autonomy.
key_factors: US tariffs cover $250B of Chinese goods; threatened escalation to 25% on $200B plus tariffs on remaining ~$267B would cover nearly all bilateral trade
China has retaliated on nearly all $130B of US imports into China, leaving limited room for further retaliation
Six MOUs under negotiation on structural issues (forced tech transfer, IP, services, currency, agriculture, non-tariff barriers) as of Feb 21, 2019
10-item purchase list being discussed including agricultural produce, energy, and semiconductors
More than half the value of China's exports to US consists of foreign components, creating collateral damage to US firms and third countries
March 1 deadline for tariff escalation likely to be extended, creating continued negotiation window
China's core demands (preserving industrial policy, state subsidies) remain unresolved and are 'quite complicated' per Chinese officials

sources_cited.excerpt: Negotiators are drawing up six memorandums of understanding on structural issues: forced technology transfer and cyber theft, intellectual property rights, services, currency, agriculture and non-tariff barriers to trade
Effective Sept. 24, President Trump announced a 10% tariff on $200 billion in Chinese imports. That tariff is currently 10%, but at the end of 2018, that's expected to rise to 25%
While China is the final assembler from many products, actually more than half of the value of those products are in parts and components from other countries like South Korea and Japan

Several Chinese government sources told Reuters that the two countries have basically reached a consensus on alleviating the trade imbalances, but there were still some differences on each other's 'core demands'
